The imposing Statue of Liberty rises proudly above New York Harbor, welcoming immigrants seeking a new life in the United States. Over time, it has become an embodiment of American ideals, freedom and the pursuit of happiness.

The Palace of Westminster's clock tower, known as Big Ben, is a cultural and historical symbol of Britain and parliamentary democracy. Built in 1859 in the Gothic Revival style, Big Ben is now the third-tallest tower in Britain.

The Colosseum, the largest amphitheatre of the ancient world, was built in the reign of Emperor Titus in the heart of Rome. Public spectacles continued to be held here even after the Roman Empire fell.
Completed in 1931, the statue of Christ the Redeemer towers over Rio de Janeiro. It is a national symbol of Brazil and holds profound significance for local Catholics.
Built in 1889, the tower is named after its chief designer, Gustave Eiffel. Standing on the Champ de Mars, it is regarded as France's foremost symbol and a source of national pride.

The Kremlin is a fortress in central Moscow. Within its walls stands the Grand Kremlin Palace, formerly a residence of the Russian emperors. The Moskva River lies to the south, Saint Basil's Cathedral and Red Square to the east, and Alexander Garden to the west. Today, the Kremlin is universally recognised as a symbol of state power.

The Reichstag, officially the Imperial Assembly Building, is the historic parliament building on Berlin's Platz der Republik. It housed the federal council until the fire of 1933. The building is an important symbol for the German people and is often associated with the country as a whole.

Since the Meiji Restoration and the overthrow of the last shogun, the Tokyo Imperial Palace has been the emperor's principal residence. It symbolises the pride and reverence of the Japanese people, inspiring them to work diligently.

The Kokkai-gijido houses both chambers of Japan's National Diet. Completed in early 1936, it was built almost entirely from Japanese materials, with few exceptions. The previous building was destroyed by a devastating fire in 1925. Although the parliament building has been destroyed repeatedly, this time it will stand for centuries!
The Hakko Ichiu Tower was erected to commemorate the 2600th anniversary of Japan's founding. The monument symbolises Japan's destiny to unite the eight corners of the world under one roof.
The Hofburg is the former residence of the Habsburg dynasty, overlooking Heldenplatz. Perhaps an Austrian ruler, whether president or king, will one day govern from here again.

The Hall of the People symbolises our people's indomitable will and their worthy ambition to dominate the world. It will show everyone that conquest can achieve anything and that our homeland can realise even seemingly impossible dreams.

Built by the Qajars and expanded by the Pahlavi dynasty, the Saadabad Complex in northern Tehran serves as the shah's residence and a centre of power. Its palaces and gardens reflect Iran's shifting political landscape, from conservatism to modernism.

The Taj Mahal is a masterpiece of Mughal architecture. Its great white marble domes and intricately designed gardens make it one of India's foremost symbols, a testament to both imperial power and historical heritage.

Standing at the crossroads of empires, Hagia Sophia has served as a Byzantine cathedral, an Ottoman mosque and a symbol of Istanbul's ever-changing rulers. Its massive dome and spacious halls reflect both its spiritual importance and the ambitions of those who sought to rule the city.
